model.label: Mandatory, community-rated basic insurance bought from competing private non-profit insurers (managed competition, with risk equalisation), plus a single-payer social insurance for long-term care

overview.statement: Since the Health Insurance Act took effect in 2006, every resident has had to buy health insurance from competing private non-profit insurers, which must offer a standard package defined by the government and must accept anyone who applies.

Statutory health insurance covers 99.9% of the population and gives access to a broad set of services, including primary, outpatient specialist and hospital care, maternity care, mental health services and ambulance transport.
The insurance obligation does not extend to everyone: certain groups such as some foreign students, undocumented migrants and asylum seekers fall outside it.

Government tracing of people without the required insurance found about 28,500 uninsured residents in 2023; people who stay uninsured or do not pay can be fined and have premiums deducted directly from wages or benefits.

locator.section: Health coverage and access: The Role of Public Health Insurance

overview.statement: The 2006 reform brought managed competition into Dutch health care and shifted the government from directly controlling volumes and prices to setting rules and overseeing the system.
In 2024 there were 20 health insurers, and the four largest held about three-quarters of the market.

locator.section: Health coverage and access: The Role of Public Health Insurance

overview.statement: Care is delivered mostly by private providers whom patients may choose freely; most GPs work in group practices or multidisciplinary centres and act as gatekeepers to most specialist care.
Long-term care runs as a separate single-payer social insurance scheme administered by the dominant insurer in each region, while municipalities are responsible for social care.

financing.statement: By law, half of the revenue for basic health insurance (Zvw) is raised through the income-related contribution, and the other half through flat-rate premiums, patients' own payments and the state's premium-replacing contribution for children (the '50/50 split').

For 2026 the health ministry projected that the €69.0 billion to be financed under basic insurance would come from €34.1 billion of income-related contributions, €28.0 billion of flat-rate premiums, €3.4 billion of state funding for children under 18 and €3.4 billion of deductible payments.
On wages and certain benefits, the income-related contribution is paid by the employer or benefit agency as an employer levy; in 2026 it is 6.10% of income up to €79,409.
On pensions and some other payments subject to wage tax, a lower contribution of 4.85% (up to the same €79,409 ceiling) is withheld from the recipient's own payment in 2026.

locator.section: 28.2.2 Bijdrage Zvw via uw nettoloon of uitkering

financing.statement: The average premium that adults pay directly to their insurer for basic cover in 2026 is €1,884 a year, or about €157 a month.
Each insurer sets its own flat premium for basic insurance, and no premium is charged for children under 18.
Insurers may charge different premiums for different plans, but within a plan every enrollee pays the same premium whatever their age or health.

locator.section: Health coverage and access: The Role of Public Health Insurance

financing.statement: Households with low and middle incomes receive a healthcare allowance (zorgtoeslag) that partly offsets the flat premium and the average deductible, so that no household pays more than a legally defined acceptable share of its income for them.
Spending on the healthcare allowance was projected at about €7.7 billion in 2026.
With a projected standard premium of €2,143 for 2026, the maximum healthcare allowance was expected to be €1,574 a year for single people and €3,010 for couples.
Of the national-insurance contributions levied on personal income in 2026, the long-term care (Wlz) contribution is 9.65% of contribution income.
The long-term care contribution rate is held constant at 9.65%, and since 2019 the long-term care fund's expected shortfalls have been covered by a state contribution (rijksbijdrage Wlz).
The state contribution to the long-term care fund was estimated at €15.2 billion for 2026.

locator.section: Artikel 8 Tegemoetkomingen en Rijksbijdragen: Rijksbijdrage Wlz

financing.statement: A second state payment to the long-term care scheme, the contribution towards the cost of tax credits (BIKK), was estimated at €6.3 billion for 2026.

Gross spending for 2026 was budgeted at €69.8 billion under basic insurance (of which €3.4 billion is paid through the deductible) and €41.9 billion under long-term care insurance (of which €2.8 billion comes from user contributions).

In 2023 government and compulsory insurance schemes paid for 83% of current health spending (EU average 80%), out-of-pocket payments for 12% (EU 16%) and voluntary health insurance for the remaining 5%.
Preventive services, including public health measures and infectious disease control, are paid for separately out of general taxation under the Public Health Act.

covered.statement: The standard package covers most primary and specialist care, medicines, medical devices, mental health care for adults, allied health services and community nursing.

Some services are left out of basic insurance, including adult dental care and physiotherapy except for certain chronic conditions; coverage rules and access to particular providers can differ between insurers.

locator.section: Health coverage and access: The Role of Public Health Insurance

covered.statement: The government decides which services basic insurance covers, reviews the list every year, and requires all insurers to offer it to every policyholder whatever their age or health.

locator.section: Health coverage and access: The Role of Public Health Insurance

covered.statement: The National Health Care Institute (Zorginstituut Nederland) reviews existing benefits on a regular basis and advises the government on what belongs in the mandatory package, with a focus on proven and appropriate care.

Three changes to the basic package took effect in 2026: stop-smoking programmes are reimbursed up to three times a year instead of once, exercise therapy for adults with severe axial spondyloarthritis is now permanently covered, and a GP's request for a specialist's advice (and an exploratory mental health consultation) no longer counts against the deductible.

For costly new hospital medicines, reimbursement is suspended when projected spending exceeds €10 million a year or €50,000 per patient while the National Health Care Institute assesses the drug's therapeutic value and cost-effectiveness; manufacturers often supply the drug free of charge during this period.

The Long-term Care Act (Wlz) covers institutional, residential and home-based care for people who need permanent supervision or have severe mental or physical disabilities, with eligibility decided by a government assessment agency on clinical need alone.
Dental care for children under 18 is part of the basic benefits package.

cost_sharing.statement: Adults pay a compulsory annual deductible of €385, the amount set for both 2026 and 2027, before insurance pays for care that falls under it.

locator.section: Wanneer u een eigen risico betaalt

cost_sharing.statement: The deductible does not apply to GP care (including out-of-hours GP posts), midwifery and maternity care, coordinated care for type 2 diabetes, COPD and cardiovascular risk, district nursing, and a combined lifestyle intervention, among other exemptions.

locator.section: Geen eigen risico voor bepaalde zorg

cost_sharing.statement: Children under 18 pay no deductible for any care in the basic package.

locator.section: Voor kinderen tot 18 jaar geen eigen risico

cost_sharing.statement: Policyholders can raise their deductible voluntarily in steps of €100 up to €500 extra in return for a lower premium, which means paying up to €885 in a year if they use care.

locator.section: Betaal ik minder premie als ik het verplichte eigen risico verhoog?

cost_sharing.statement: In 2024, 85% of enrollees chose no voluntary deductible, while about 10% chose the maximum.
Since 2019, co-payments on prescription medicines have been capped at €250 a year, with insurers reimbursing anything above the cap; the cap is separate from the deductible.
The government has extended the €250 annual cap on co-payments for outpatient medicines through 2027.

locator.section: Beleidsagenda: eigen risico en eigen bijdragen

cost_sharing.statement: In 2023, outpatient medical care accounted for 38% of out-of-pocket spending (EU average 17%) and retail medicines for 17% (EU average 26%).
Some people with minimum-wage incomes do not pay the mandatory deductible because they are covered through collective insurance packages arranged by municipalities.
For residential long-term care, users pay a copayment linked to income and wealth of up to €2,954 a month.

financial_hardship.statement: Statistics Netherlands counted 181,720 adults in arrears on their health insurance premium at the end of 2025 (provisional), up from 166,070 at the end of 2023 but well below 282,190 at the end of 2015.

locator.table: 81062ned: persons with premium arrears, men and women, 18 and older, by year (31 December)

financial_hardship.statement: People six or more months behind on their premium are reported by their insurer to the CAK defaulter scheme, which imposes an administrative premium, deducted from income where possible; they remain insured for basic cover.

locator.section: Wat gebeurt er als ik mijn zorgverzekering niet betaal?

financial_hardship.statement: Growing pressure on household finances has led more people to avoid care for financial reasons, according to the Commonwealth Fund's profile.

additional_care.statement: In 2025, 80.6% of people with basic insurance also bought some form of supplementary private insurance.

locator.section: The Role of Private Health Insurance

additional_care.statement: Most supplementary plans pay for services that basic insurance excludes or only partly covers, such as dental care, physiotherapy, eye care, contraceptives, care abroad and alternative medicine, and they can reduce or fully cover copayments.

locator.section: The Role of Private Health Insurance

additional_care.statement: Depending on the package, supplementary insurance can give access to a wider network of providers and quicker specialist appointments than basic insurance alone.

locator.section: The Role of Private Health Insurance

additional_care.statement: Within basic insurance, plans with higher premiums generally allow more freedom to choose providers, while cheaper plans restrict the choice.
Patients who see a specialist without a GP referral must use private insurance or pay out of pocket.
Premiums for supplementary insurance are set by the insurer, and no income-related government contribution is levied on them.

access.statement: In 2024 only 1.6% of people needing medical care reported unmet needs because of cost, distance or waiting times, under half the EU average of 3.5%; among people at risk of poverty the figure was 4.3%.
In a 2024 Eurofound survey, 9% of adults needing mental health care reported an unmet need, above the EU average of 7%.

In 2024 about two-thirds of patients referred to specialist mental health services waited more than four weeks for a first consultation, and almost 40% waited more than ten weeks for treatment to start.
About 78,000 people were on mental health waiting lists at the end of 2023, with limited capacity and a shortage of professionals, especially in children's services, cited as reasons.
A GP appointment can usually be had within two days, and nearly the whole population lives within 15 minutes' travel of a GP.
GPs can turn away new patients and practice lists are capped, and 60% of GP practices stopped taking new patients in 2024.
In 2023 there were 3.9 practising doctors per 1,000 people, up from 3.4 in 2014 but below the EU average of 4.3; about one in four doctors is a GP.
Nurse numbers rose from 10.3 per 1,000 people in 2014 to 11.1 in 2023, above the EU average of 8.4.

Waiting times for hip and knee replacement fell in 2023 and again in 2024 to near pre-pandemic levels, but waits for cataract surgery rose in 2023, eased only slightly in 2024 and stayed well above pre-pandemic levels.
GPs must provide 50 hours of after-hours care a year, paid separately, and local and regional GP posts provide out-of-hours care that reduces the need for emergency room visits.

locator.section: How Countries Did on Each Performance Domain: Access to care

access.statement: Hospital beds fell from 3.2 per 1,000 people in 2017 to 2.3 in 2023, less than half the EU average of 5.1, reflecting the emphasis on outpatient care and GP gatekeeping.

outcomes.statement: Life expectancy at birth was 82 years in 2024, four months above the EU average; it has recovered from the pandemic more slowly than the EU average and is still below pre-pandemic levels.
In 2022 mortality from treatable causes was 34% lower than the EU average, and mortality from preventable causes 21% lower.
In 2023 the Netherlands had among the lowest 30-day mortality rates in the EU after hospital admission: 5.0 deaths per 100 patients for heart attack and 9.3 for ischaemic stroke.
In 2023 combined hospital admission rates for diabetes, congestive heart failure, asthma and COPD were 29% below the EU average, though the rate for asthma and COPD alone was slightly above average.
Breast cancer screening among women aged 50-69 fell from 77% in 2018 to 70% in 2023, continuing a decline since 2007.
First-dose measles vaccination fell to 89% of children in 2024, below the EU average of 92% and the 95% needed for herd immunity.
In the GBD 2019 study, the Netherlands' Healthcare Access and Quality (HAQ) Index score for ages 0-74 was 91.1 (95% uncertainty interval 88.7-92.6) in 2019, 16.0 points higher than in 1990.

locator.table: Table: HAQ Index estimates by location; row values in order: 2019 overall (0-74 years), young (0-14), working (15-64), post-working (65-74), then absolute change 1990-2019 for the same four groups

outcomes.statement: Five-year survival for prostate, breast, cervical, colon and lung cancer and for childhood leukaemia is above the EU average, partly because of successful screening programmes.
Dutch women live shorter lives than women in the EU on average, partly because of higher smoking rates in the past.
Between 2015 and 2018, people with the least education lived on average 6.3 years less than the most highly educated.

costs.statement: In 2023 health spending was 9.8% of GDP, slightly under the EU average of 10%, but spending per person (EUR 4,848, adjusted for purchasing power) was 26% above the EU average and the fourth highest in the EU after Norway, Germany and Austria.
Long-term care took 29% of health spending in 2023, far above the EU average of 18%.

After real-terms rises of over 10% in 2020 and nearly 8% in 2021, public health spending fell by over 6% in 2022 and 1% in 2023, and health's share of government spending dropped from 18% in 2021 to 16% in 2023, one point below its pre-pandemic level.

Retail pharmaceutical spending was EUR 6.7 billion in 2023, or EUR 309 per person adjusted for purchasing power, the lowest in the EU, because people use fewer medicines and pay lower prices for them.
Generics made up 79% of the medicine units dispensed by community pharmacies in 2023, up from 67% in 2012 and among the highest shares in the EU.
In 2021 the average hospital stay was 4.3 days, the shortest in the EU, compared with 5.9 days in Belgium and 8.9 in Germany.
The average annual premium for basic insurance rose from about €1,400 in 2020 to about €1,900 in 2025, faster than inflation and faster than the healthcare allowance for lower-income people.

locator.section: Health coverage and access: The Role of Public Health Insurance

costs.statement: Treatable mortality is very low, but the Netherlands spends considerably more per person than several EU countries with similar treatable mortality rates.

what_works.statement: In Mirror, Mirror 2024, the Netherlands, the UK and Germany performed best on access to care, helped by low cost-related barriers reported by patients and minimal out-of-pocket costs.

locator.section: How Countries Did on Each Performance Domain: Access to care

what_works.statement: Primary care's main strengths are accessibility and quality: GP care is exempt from the compulsory deductible, which keeps it quick to reach.
The Netherlands has the lowest antibiotic consumption in the EU, consistently around half the EU average.
Day surgery has expanded: the share of tonsillectomies done as day cases rose from 70% in 2015 to 85% in 2021, and of inguinal hernia repairs from 81% to 87%.

For medicines approved in the EU between 2020 and 2023, reimbursement took 459 days on average, about four months faster than the EU average of 578, and 58% of them were reimbursed by January 2025 (EU average 43%).
In 2022 the Netherlands invested about EUR 14 million per 100,000 people in health ICT equipment, software and databases, the most of any EU country.

problems.statement: GP shortages are growing and expected to worsen as many GPs near retirement or leave early, and shortages also affect psychiatry, paediatrics and geriatrics.

Vacancy rates have risen across health care, most of all for nurses, psychologists and GPs, and projections suggest meeting care needs could take 20% of the labour force by 2030 and over 30% by 2060 if trends continue.
Surveyed GPs worked 48 hours a week on average in 2024, four hours more than in 2018 and 2013, and all of the extra time went on tasks not related to patients.
Very low generic prices make the Dutch market unattractive to suppliers and have led to more frequent temporary medicine shortages over the past decade.

A 2024 review of 15 years of regulated competition concluded that the high expectations of the 2006 market reform have not been met and that the system works much less like a market than its framing suggests.
The conditions for efficient competition among insurers are not fully met, partly because of the complex system of risk adjustment among insurers.
Although insurers can negotiate on quality, most of their contracts with providers are still based more on volume and price than on quality.
Price negotiations for medicines held back under the cost-control procedure can drag on, leaving some medicines unreimbursed even while supplied for free, which manufacturers increasingly resist.

In its 2025 budget the government announced a EUR 300 million cut to funding for pandemic preparedness and infectious disease control, which municipal health services fear could seriously weaken future public health protection.
GP-based mental health services are covered without the deductible, but inpatient and ambulatory mental health care count against it, which may further limit access.
Access to some expensive medicines for rare diseases is restricted, and some residents are uninsured or default on premiums, although overall coverage gaps are low.

reforms.statement: In its 2027 budget the government said the compulsory deductible, unchanged at €385 since 2016, should again move with care costs, and it postponed a planned €60 increase from 2027 to 2028.

locator.section: Beleidsagenda: eigen risico en eigen bijdragen

reforms.statement: The government is preparing to limit the deductible to at most €150 per specialist-care treatment, to take effect in 2028 after a one-year implementation period.

locator.section: Beleidsagenda: eigen risico en eigen bijdragen

reforms.statement: To contain costs the government plans user charges for youth care and district nursing, and from 2029 will no longer provide household help as an individually assessed municipal service.

locator.section: Beleidsagenda: eigen risico en eigen bijdragen

reforms.statement: The coalition agreement underlying the 2027 budget includes a measure not to lower the deductible and to index it from 2027.

locator.table: Belangrijkste beleidsmatige uitgavenmutaties Zvw: Mutaties coalitieakkoord

reforms.statement: The four-party coalition in office from mid-2024 had planned, citing unequal access to care, to lower the deductible to €165 from 2027 and to cap it at €50 per hospital treatment.

In October 2025 the competition authority (ACM), the Dutch Healthcare Authority (NZa) and the National Health Care Institute jointly proposed a framework for judging when prices of high-cost medicines are socially acceptable.
Since January 2025 the authorities have applied stricter rules to clarify work relationships and steer freelance nurses towards stable salaried jobs.

In 2025 the health ministry launched a National Vision and Strategy on the Health Information System to modernise health data infrastructure so that medical information is available and usable for patients, providers, researchers and policymakers.

The Integrated Care Agreement (IZA) concluded in 2022-23 sets out about 400 agreements on appropriate care, regional cooperation, primary care, links between social, primary and mental health care, prevention, workforce and digitalisation.

Since 1 January 2022 adult mental health care has been financed through a fee-for-service system in which providers are reimbursed only for consultations and inpatient days, at maximum prices set by the Dutch Healthcare Authority.
Legislation in 2023 gave more options to regulate care providers in order to prevent fraud such as upcoding or billing for care not delivered.

The 2015 reform of non-acute care introduced the Long-term Care Act, the Youth Act and the Social Support Act, aiming to reduce inpatient nursing care and help people live at home longer, and it came with a significant cut in the total budget.

us_lessons.statement: Mirror, Mirror 2024, written to draw lessons for the US, suggests that countries seeking to fix problems of access to care could look to the Netherlands.

locator.section: What the U.S. Can Do to Improve

us_lessons.statement: In Mirror, Mirror 2024, Australia and the Netherlands ranked highest overall while spending the lowest share of GDP on health, whereas the US spent far more of its GDP and performed worst.

A comparison of risk adjustment in Germany, the Netherlands and the US ACA Marketplaces found in all three that the most under- and overpaid enrollees tend to remain so the following year, making these payment errors predictable and a potential source of risk selection by insurers.

The same three-country study proposed combining risk pooling with reinsurance aimed at enrollees predicted to be undercompensated, and found that this substantially improved how well payments matched spending in Germany, the Netherlands and the US Marketplaces alike.
